3. Katie Taylor vs Amanda Serrano I, 30 April 2022, round 3, "01:14-01:18 of the round".

message.content: On it. I'm checking Ludo's three reference jabs, the free mocap sources, and his timing claims now. I'll paste the full answer with sources when it's done.
The J63 check is running now. I'll paste the full answer here and attach the file when it's done.

I've checked Ludo's three reference jabs. All three fights' dates, venues and rounds are right, but none of his three timestamps could be confirmed. I can't watch video, so a person needs to scrub each moment.

Of his biomechanics claims, the extension time and the shoulder lift hold up. The retraction claim is backwards: measured retraction is about 2x slower than extension, not faster. I found no source at all for the 15 ms heel drop. The full memo is below and attached.

## 1. Holmes vs Cooney, 11 Jun 1982, round 2
- **Facts confirmed** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Holmes_vs._Gerry_Cooney)): Caesars Palace, Las Vegas, WBC and Ring heavyweight titles, referee Mills Lane. Holmes dropped Cooney in round 2 and won by TKO in round 13 when Cooney's trainer threw in the towel. Both fighters are orthodox. HBO re-aired the fight a week later.
- **Video:** I found no official HBO upload. Fan full-fight uploads came up in search but weren't load-checked: `-ZFgK1lIU8M` (the Howard Cosell version), `6s2rOOocTXs` and `_tBqID-E68I`.
- **"04:18 on the HBO reel": NOT CONFIRMED.** No official reel turned up. On a full upload, 04:18 would usually still be in the intros or round 1, so Ludo needs to name the exact video ID.
- **Angle:** a high, wide side angle at standard definition is likely, but that's my inference.

## 2. Golovkin vs Lemieux, 17 Oct 2015, round 1
- **Facts confirmed:** Madison Square Garden on HBO PPV, referee Steve Willis. Lemieux went down in round 5 and Golovkin won by TKO at 1:32 of round 8. There was no knockdown in round 1. GGG is orthodox.
- **Official video that loads:** [DAZN Rewind full fight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zI_k8cDCV1E).
- **Ludo's timestamp:** "2:44–2:48 of the round" is possible. "09:12 on the tape" is unverified, because it depends on how long the intros run. In the corner after round 1, Abel Sanchez says "very good jab", so GGG's jab was landing that round.

## 3. Taylor vs Serrano I, 30 Apr 2022, round 3
- **Facts confirmed:** MSG on DAZN, undisputed lightweight titles. Taylor won a split decision (94–96, 97–93, 96–93) over 10 two-minute rounds, with no knockdowns.
- **Stance:** Taylor is orthodox and Serrano is a southpaw, so this is an open-stance jab on a different line from the other two. Don't use it as the generic jab without noting that.
- **Official video:** [Matchroom full fight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Vqjc10kai4) is 22:38 and probably cut down (most likely without the breaks). There's also a [DAZN playlist copy](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLqbKSibnZu3fEtWNjrpMAni8TdGdeC88X).
- **Ludo's timestamp:** "1:14–1:18 of round 3" fits inside a 2-minute round, but whether a jab actually lands there is unverified.

**How a person finds the clean jab:**
1. Use the official upload, convert the round time to the video time, and scrub ±10 s at 0.25× speed.
2. Pick a fully side-on jab that the referee isn't blocking and that returns cleanly to guard.
3. Log the video ID, the video time and the round clock.
4. Check by eye: chamber, extension line, fist turn, shoulder lift, rear-hand guard, lead heel and retraction.

Broadcast video runs at 30 or 60 fps, which is 17–33 ms per frame, so a 15 ms heel drop can't be seen on it anyway.

## Freely usable jab references
| Source | Licence | Jab? |
|---|---|---|
| [CMU Graphics Lab Mocap](https://mocap.cs.cmu.edu/) | Custom CMU terms: free for research, can ship inside commercial products, can't be resold as raw data, and acknowledgement is requested. Not a named open licence. | Boxing trials 13_17, 13_18, 14_01–03, 15_13 and 17_10. Subject 144 ("punching female", 120 fps) has Left_Punch_Sequence001/002. None are labelled "jab", but left punches by an orthodox subject are likely jabs. Start with subject 144, since the low-numbered subjects are lower quality. |
| [Adobe Mixamo](https://helpx.adobe.com/creative-cloud/faq/mixamo-faq.html) | Adobe terms: royalty-free in commercial games with no attribution, but the raw files can't be redistributed. | It has punch and boxing clips, but I didn't confirm a clip actually named "jab". |
| [BoxingVI dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16524) | No licence stated. It's annotations over 20 YouTube videos, so the footage keeps its original copyright. | Yes: 6,915 punch clips including jabs, with 2D pose. Fine for study only. |

Rokoko free packs, AIST++ and Human3.6M weren't checked this pass. From memory, AIST++ is dance only and Human3.6M is non-commercial academic use only, but treat both as unverified. CMU is the best candidate for commercial use, though legal should confirm the custom terms.

## Ludo's timing claims
| Claim | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Extension 120–140 ms | [Sensors 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/21/23/7882), wearable sensor on jabs into a heavy bag: throw phase 117 ± 25 ms for experienced boxers and 135 ms for inexperienced | Roughly supported |
| Retraction 90–110 ms, about 1.25x faster | Same study: retraction 262 ± 42 ms experienced, 212 ± 75 ms inexperienced; whole jab 485–524 ms | Contradicted: retraction is about 2x slower |
| Heel drops about 15 ms before contact | Nothing found. [Whiting et al. 1988](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3377096/) found arm speed peaks 8–21 ms before contact, which is about the arm, not the heel | Unsupported, possibly a mix-up with Whiting |
| Shoulder rises to cover the chin | Coaching description in the [J Phys Ed Sport 2022 jab study](https://doi.org/10.7752/jpes.2022.03083) | Supported as coaching, not as a measured value |

**More measured data:**
- [Piorkowski et al. 2011](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14763141.2010.547590), 10 competition boxers in optical mocap: straight punches took 357 ± 178 ms from start to contact, with contact speed of 9.3 m/s.
- [Kimm & Thiel 2015](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proeng.2015.07.232), 16 amateurs: air-jab peak speed 8.1 m/s for men and 6.6 m/s for women, with no durations given.
- **Not retrieved:** Atha 1985 and Lenetsky.

**For the animators:** use about 115–135 ms for extension. Make retraction equal to or slower than extension, unless it's deliberately a snap-back air jab. Drop the 15 ms heel rule or label it a design choice, and keep the shoulder lift.

**Not covered:** Rokoko, AIST++, Human3.6M, Atha, Lenetsky, coaching breakdowns of each fighter's jab, and every frame-level detail and timestamp.

# J63 (S238) for John: when should a boxing coach CHANGE THE PLAN? Sourced signs and thresholds for a gains/attrition meter

Discipline: boxing (demo). No MMA, kickboxing or team-sport-only sources unless you flag them as such.

## Why
The operator wants the game's training loop built around two meters, GAINS and ATTRITION, which tell the player when to change
a fighter's training plan. Our lead designer proposed thresholds (acute fatigue over 75%, CNS stress over 80%, injury risk over
25%) with NO sources. We need real ones, or an honest "no number exists - here is the best proxy".

## Questions (answer each, with sources, a confidence level and the population behind it)
1. What signs do real boxing coaches and S&C staff use to decide a fighter is going stale or overreached in camp (session-RPE
   trends, morning HR/HRV, mood questionnaires such as POMS/RESTQ/Hooper index, grip or jump tests, sleep, sparring
   performance, weight)? Which are practical day to day?
2. Thresholds: for each usable sign, the published cut-off or change that marks functional overreaching (FOR),
   non-functional overreaching (NFOR) and overtraining (OTS) - e.g. Hooper index rise, HRV drop % vs baseline, CMJ drop %,
   sRPE weekly load rise %, monotony/strain (Foster). Say which come from combat sports and which are borrowed.
3. Gains flattening: how fast do boxing-relevant qualities improve over a 4-8 week camp (aerobic, punch force/speed,
   technique) and how quickly do they plateau or drop when load is too high? Typical % per week if any study gives it.
4. Recovery: after an NFOR warning, how many days of reduced load do coaches use, and how much does load drop?
5. Coaching effect: any evidence that a coach present (supervised training) changes adaptation or injury rates vs
   unsupervised training (any sport; flag it)?
6. The one-line rule a real boxing coach would give: "pull him off when ...".

## Format
Markdown memo. A "Key sources" list with links first, then one section per question, then a TABLE: sign | FOR | NFOR | OTS |
source | population | confidence. Say plainly what was NOT found. No invented numbers.

## Prior research
J62_TRAINING_DAY_REPLY.md (session-RPE load, Gabbett16 ACWR and its critiques Impellizzeri20/Lolli19, McCabe23 elite amateur
camp, BoxSci tapering) and J_STRESS_S206.md (the FOR/NFOR/OTS ladder, non-training stress). Build on them; do not repeat them.

## What would a human do?
A boxing coach watches the fighter's sharpness on the pads, asks how he slept, checks his weight and resting heart rate in the
morning, and cuts the session short or gives him a rest day when the snap is gone two days running.

## Prefab check
Not applicable (research only).

message.content: On it. I'm starting the research on when to change the plan now: staleness signs, the FOR, NFOR and OTS thresholds, how fast gains flatten, recovery blocks, the effect of coach supervision, and the coach's one-line rule. I'll paste the full memo with sources when it's done.
The J63 (S238) research is running now. I'll paste the full memo, including the sign and threshold table, and attach the file when it's done.

J63 (S238) is done. No published number separates functional overreaching (FOR) from non-functional overreaching (NFOR) and overtraining (OTS). The only consensus test is how long performance takes to come back: days to about 2 weeks is FOR, weeks to months is NFOR, and months with other causes ruled out is OTS (Meeusen 2013). None of Ludo's three thresholds (75 / 80 / 25%) has a source, so each is mapped to its best proxy below. The full memo is attached.

**Caveat:** I checked the boxing studies live, but the figures from the classic monitoring papers (Meeusen, Hooper, Foster, Plews, Buchheit, Claudino, Saw, Bosquet, Mazzetti, Coutts, Gentil, Lacroix) were written from memory and not re-opened. Check each exact figure before it goes into game text. McCabe 2023 (covered in earlier work) and the weight-cut studies are not in this pass.

## Key sources
[Meeusen 2013 consensus](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23247672/), [Hooper 1995](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7898325/), [Foster 1998](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9662690/), [Plews 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22367011/), [Plews 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23852425/), [Buchheit 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3936188/), [Claudino 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27663764/), [Gathercole 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24912201/), [Saw 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26423706/), [Baumert 2006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17016118/), [Shanghai boxing HRV abstract](https://doi.org/10.14428/ebr.v1i4.8973), [Kamandulis 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28800004/), [Frontiers 2026 boxing repeated-sprint study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2026.1839505/full), [Boxing HIIT 2021](https://doi.org/10.3390/su13168746), [Chaabene 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25358529/), [Slimani 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27304196/), [Bosquet 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17762369/), [Mazzetti 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10862549/), [Coutts 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15142024/), [Gentil 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3761809/), [Lacroix 2017](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28573401/).

## 1. Signs of staleness, and which work day to day
- **Wellness questionnaires (Hooper, POMS, RESTQ):** Saw 2016 reviewed 56 studies across mixed sports. Self-reported wellness tracked load changes more reliably than blood, heart-rate or VO2 measures. A Hooper-style form takes under a minute and works daily, while POMS and RESTQ are better weekly. Confidence is high that they track load and low that they diagnose NFOR.
- **Morning HRV/HR:** use a 7-day rolling average, not single readings (Plews, Buchheit; endurance athletes, borrowed). The only boxing data is an abstract on 16 Shanghai boxers after a 4-week heavy block: LF/HF rose from 1.6 to 2.5 and tracked morning pulse, CK and T/C, with no thresholds given. It works daily with a chest strap. Confidence is medium, and low for boxing.
- **Jump test (CMJ):** the average height across several jumps picks up fatigue better than the best jump (Claudino 2017). It's practical 2–3 times a week. I found no study using it to monitor boxers in camp. Confidence is medium.
- **Grip strength:** I found no evidence it detects overreaching. Confidence is low.
- **Sleep:** it's part of most wellness forms. No boxing threshold was found.
- **Sparring and pad performance:** a drop in performance that persists despite rest is the defining sign of NFOR (Meeusen). No boxing test has been validated for this, so the coach's eye is the real tool. Confidence is low.
- **Weight:** it's confounded by the weight cut, and no threshold exists.

**Practical daily set:** wellness, morning HRV or HR, and session-RPE. Add a jump test 2–3 times a week and a weekly set drill on the bag or pads.

## 2. Thresholds
| Sign | FOR | NFOR | OTS | Source | Population | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance (pads, bag, sparring output) | Drops, back within days to ~2 weeks | Still down after ~2 weeks, for weeks to months | Down for months, other causes excluded | Meeusen 2013 | Consensus, all sports | High (it's the definition) |
| Hooper/wellness | Rises with load, falls when load drops | Stays high; no number | No number | Hooper 1995, Saw 2016 | Elite swimmers; mixed review (borrowed) | Medium for the trend, low for a number |
| HRV (7-day average of lnRMSSD) | About −24% RMSSD in a 2-week camp, back in 3–4 days | 7-day average below the smallest worthwhile change (0.5 × the athlete's own SD) for a sustained stretch, with day-to-day variation falling (one case report) | No number; can even rise | Baumert 2006, Plews 2012/13, Buchheit 2014 | Track athletes and triathletes (borrowed) | Medium |
| HRV in boxers | LF/HF up from 1.6 to 2.5 after a 4-week heavy block | Not found | Not found | Shanghai abstract | 16 male boxers | Low |
| Jump test (average height) | Below the athlete's own typical error, then recovers | No agreed % | No agreed % | Claudino 2017, Gathercole 2015 | Mixed sports; rugby (borrowed) | Low for numbers |
| Monotony | Above about 2.0 under high load is a warning | Not separated | Not separated | Foster 1998 | Mixed athletes (borrowed) | Medium |
| Strain | Individual only | — | — | Foster 1998 | Mixed (borrowed) | Low |
| Weekly load rise | The "≤10%" rule is folklore | — | — | None | — | Low |
| Grip, weight, sleep | No thresholds found | — | — | — | — | Low |

## 3. How fast gains come, and when they flatten
- **Frontiers 2026** (16 elite male boxers, 4 weeks of boxing-specific repeated sprints): peak punch speed +7.3%, average punch speed +14.9%, punches in 30 s +16.8%, upper-body Wingate peak power +16.7%. Spread evenly, that's about **2–5% a week** (my own arithmetic from a small sample, so treat it as an upper bound).
- **Kamandulis 2018** (18 amateur boxers, 4 weeks): VO2peak, punch force and staying power across rounds all improved. The abstract gives no % figures.
- **Boxing HIIT 2021** (16 national-level boxers, 4 weeks): VO2max gain was small (effect size 0.42), punch output in simulated bouts was moderate (0.56), and the jump test was unchanged.
- **Not found:** how fast technique improves during a camp, and any boxing study measuring a plateau. Borrowed picture: in FOR, performance rebounds after the load drops, and in NFOR it doesn't come back for weeks. Model fast early gains with diminishing returns, not a straight line over 8 weeks.

## 4. Recovery after an NFOR warning
- Heart-rate measures recovered in 3–4 days after a 2-week camp (Baumert, track athletes and triathletes, borrowed).
- If recovery takes about 2 weeks or less, it was FOR. Beyond that it's NFOR, which takes weeks to months (Meeusen).
- How much to cut has no trial behind it. The best proxy is taper research (Bosquet 2007): cut volume by 41–60% and keep intensity and frequency, for about 2 weeks. For suspected NFOR or OTS, Meeusen recommends rest and a medical check, with no fixed %.

## 5. Does coach supervision matter?
None of these studies is from boxing; all are resistance training. Supervised groups gained more strength in Mazzetti 2000 (trained men, who also chose heavier loads), Coutts 2004 (young rugby league players), Gentil 2010 (untrained men) and the Lacroix 2017 meta-analysis (older adults). **No trial shows that supervision reduces injury.** So a coach bonus to gains is defensible, but a coach bonus against injury is a design choice.

## 6. The coach's one-liner
I found no real coach quote that gives a rule. This paraphrase of the evidence is mine, not a citation: "Pull him off when he's flat on the pads and bag for more than a few days and says he's sleeping badly and always tired. One bad day is fatigue; a week of it is a problem."

## Mapping Ludo's three thresholds
- **Acute fatigue above 75%:** no source. Drive it from wellness or HRV more than about 1 SD worse than the boxer's own baseline for 3 or more days, which flags FOR. That 1 SD is a common practitioner convention, not a validated cut-off. If it clears after 3–4 easy days, fine. If it lasts past about 14 days with a performance drop, he's in NFOR. Keep 75% only as a UI tier labelled a design value.
- **CNS stress above 80%:** no validated measure exists. Rename it "neuromuscular fatigue" and drive it from a jump-test drop and HRV below the smallest worthwhile change, or from monotony above 2.0 under high load (Foster, the only proxy with a real threshold).
- **Injury risk above 25%:** nothing supports a percentage injury chance from load data. Keep it as a design value that rises with sustained high strain, high monotony and NFOR status.
- **Recovery:** FOR means 3–7 lighter days. An NFOR warning means about 2 weeks at 40–60% less volume, keeping intensity. Confirmed NFOR means weeks off, and OTS means months, which takes him out of camp.
- **Gains:** about 2–5% a week for the first 4 weeks of a new stimulus, then diminishing returns, with gains paused while in NFOR.

# CLIPREVIEW1 - review our boxing fight motion (FightCamp, S259)

FightCamp is a PC boxing-gym management sim: you train a boxer, book his fight, and WATCH the bout as a 3D simulation (two
MetaHuman-style boxers, red trunks vs blue trunks, game camera high and three-quarter, like a broadcast). The operator watched our
latest fight clip and said: "The 3d fight looks terrible torso twists weird legs fly not walk" and "the jab fires like bullet why is
it so fast". We changed the motion system (one writer moves each body per frame instead of eight) and need every reviewer's eyes.

## The clip, in numbers (seed 95501, 40 s, 1,200 frames per boxer; left = before, right = after the change)
| measure | before red/blue | after red/blue |
|---|---|---|
| frames a PLANTED foot slides on the canvas | 315 / 333 | 186 / 161 (13-15%; goal <= 5%) |
| body root moving > 4 m/s (teleport-like) | 8 / 9 | 0 / 0 |
| body root moving > 1.5 m/s | 231 / 229 | 140 / 66 |
| hips lower than 0.70 m (crouched) | 159 / 39 | 116 / 5 |
| feet more than 0.95 m apart | 42 / 44 | 25 / 29 |
| torso twist > 50 deg (red) | 17 | 19 |
| centre-to-centre distance the engine holds in exchanges | 0.557 m - torsos visibly merge | same |

What the frames (every 2 s) show after the change: the red boxer often crouches with bent knees and leans forward into the blue
man; in exchanges the two torsos touch or overlap; bare feet; gloves red; the blue man stands taller and more upright.
The jab: from guard to full extension the glove travels in a very short time - the operator says it "fires like a bullet".

## Questions (answer every one, as long and specific as you can)
1. Which reads more like two real boxers - and where exactly does the motion break (feet, hips, torso twist, spacing)?
2. Feet: real boxing footwork is push-step, pivot, shuffle - never a glide. What should planted feet do during a punch? When must
   a foot move, and how far, in a real jab, cross, hook? Give numbers where you know them.
3. Punch speed: real numbers for an elite and an amateur boxer - jab fist peak speed (m/s), time from guard to full extension (s),
   time back to guard, and how this changes for cross, hook, uppercut. How fast should a VIDEO GAME show it so it reads well to a
   viewer (games often slow punches down - which ones do, by how much)?
4. Spacing: what distance between the two boxers' chest centres in an exchange (jab range, hook range, clinch)? What stops
   torsos merging in fighting games (collision capsules, push-out, animation spacing)?
5. Name the three most important things to fix first, in order, and what a fighting-game animator would do about each.

## Your angle
JOHN (research): real-boxing reference - cite measured studies (punch velocity papers, motion-capture of boxers, footwork biomechanics). Numbers first.

Write the longest complete answer you can. Plain words, numbers with units, sources where you have them.

message.content: On it. I'm pulling the measured boxing numbers now: footwork, punch speed and timing, spacing between the two boxers, and how fighting games keep torsos from merging. I'll paste the full CLIPREVIEW1 answer with sources when it's done.
The CLIPREVIEW1 research is running now. I'll paste the full answer to all five questions here and attach the file when it's done.

CLIPREVIEW1 is done. The "after" clip reads better, but it still isn't two real boxers. The biggest break is spacing: the engine holds 0.557 m between the boxers, while elite boxers average 1.23 m apart. The real jab is about as fast as ours, and it looks like a bullet because nothing comes before it or after it. Full answer below, file attached.

## 1. Before vs after, and where the motion breaks
Each figure is a share of 1,200 frames per boxer, red / blue.

| Measure | Before | After | Real benchmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| Planted foot sliding | 26% / 28% | 15.5% / 13.4% | About 0% outside deliberate pivots; goal ≤5% |
| Root above 4 m/s | 0.7% | 0% | Ring average about 0.86 m/s (estimate: 155 m per round ÷ 180 s, French elite boxers, [S1]) |
| Root above 1.5 m/s | 19% | 11.7% / 5.5% | Short bursts only (steps, lunges). Burst speed NOT FOUND |
| Hips below 0.70 m | 13% / 3% | 9.7% / 0.4% | Stance hips about 0.78–0.88 m for a 1.78 m boxer (estimate) |
| Feet more than 0.95 m apart | 3.5% | 2.1% / 2.4% | About 0.45–0.75 m (estimate from shoulder width) |
| Red torso twist above 50° | 17 frames | 19 frames | Above 50° is plausible only if the pelvis turns too |
| Distance between boxers in exchanges | 0.557 m | 0.557 m | 1.23 ± 0.16 m, elite mean [S1] |

**The four breaks:**
- **Feet:** they still slide 13–15% of the time.
- **Red's crouch:** red is too low and drives forward into blue (116 frames of deep crouch). Deep crouches should happen only on ducks and slips.
- **Spacing:** torsos overlap at 0.56 m against a real 1.23 m.
- **Twist:** it comes from the spine instead of the hips. Experienced boxers turn the pelvis and thighs, while novices twist the spine ([Izumi 2018](https://core.ac.uk/download/223208425.pdf): "trunk rotation, not trunk twist"). In elite boxers the trunk contributes only 6.7% of the cross ([Dinu & Louis 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7739747/)). Red's twist got worse while everything else improved, which suggests the spine alone is doing it.

**Correction to my earlier memos:** the ~43° jab / ~73° trunk-rotation figures I cited in J63 and J67 couldn't be re-confirmed in this pass. Treat them as unverified until someone opens that 2026 BMC paper.

## 2. Feet during each punch
- **Jab:** weight loads onto the rear foot, the rear leg drives, and the lead foot unloads and steps ([Lenetsky 2020](https://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr/fulltext/2020/04000/defining_the_phases_of_boxing_punches__a.22.aspx)). The jab is the only punch with a significant force difference between the legs ([Stanley 2018](https://doi.org/10.1080/24748668.2018.1525651), 15 amateurs). For a step-jab, the lead foot moves about 10–30 cm (estimate; the measured length was NOT FOUND) and the rear foot slides up the same amount afterwards. In a standing jab, neither foot moves.
- **Cross:** ground force splits 60.6% lead / 39.4% rear in elite boxers and 54.1% / 45.9% in juniors (Dinu). The rear heel lifts and the rear foot pivots on the ball, which stays in place. A measured pivot angle was NOT FOUND.
- **Hook:** the lead foot pivots on the ball with the heel turning out. No force imbalance between the legs was found. Angle NOT FOUND.
- **Uppercut:** the knees dip and drive up, both feet stay planted, and there's a slight pivot on the punching side.
- **Engine rule:** the ball of a planted foot never moves. It may only pivot or lift its heel. A foot moves only in an explicit step (step-jab, advance, retreat, circling) of about 10–30 cm, taking about 4–6 frames at 30 fps (estimate). Outside those step windows, a 0% slide target is realistic.

## 3. Punch speed
| Punch | Number | Population and source |
|---|---|---|
| Jab, guard to contact | **117 ± 25 ms** experienced; 135 ± 42 ms inexperienced | 11 experienced and 20 inexperienced boxers, [Sensors 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/21/23/7882) |
| Jab, back to guard | **262 ± 42 ms** experienced; 212 ± 75 ms inexperienced; whole jab about 0.49–0.52 s | same |
| Jab delivery | 405 ms | 15 amateurs, Stanley 2018 |
| All punches, peak fist speed | 6.6–12.5 m/s, reached 8–21 ms before contact | 4 experienced boxers, [Whiting 1988](https://doi.org/10.1177/036354658801600207) |
| Maximal punch | 9.26 ± 2.09 m/s at contact; hooks faster than jab or cross | 10 competition boxers, [Piorkowski 2011](https://knowledge.lancashire.ac.uk/id/eprint/3757/1/piorkowski-et-al-2011-punch-kinematics.pdf) |
| Cross | 8.1 m/s elite and junior; 8.48 ± 0.61 m/s | Dinu; [boxing vs sanda study, 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11466798/) |
| Hook | **11.2 ± 2.0** elite, 8.9 junior; lead hook 11.95 m/s | Dinu; Stanley |
| Uppercut | **10.2 ± 1.8** elite, 7.3 junior | Dinu |

A clean jab-only peak speed, and the papers by Smith, Walilko, Atha and Kimm read first-hand, were NOT FOUND in this pass.

**Why it fires like a bullet:** a real 117 ms jab is only 3.5 frames at 30 fps. Real footage sells it with a weight shift beforehand, a step, and a long, slow return of about 8 frames.

**What games do:**
- **Street Fighter 6:** Ken's jab is 4 frames startup, 3 active and 7 recovery at 60 fps, about 0.23 s in total ([SF6 frame data](https://sf6-lab.net/en/fighters/ken/frame)).
- **Tekken 8:** the jab hits on frame 10 (about 167 ms), followed by 17–19 recovery frames ([Wavu Wiki](https://wavu.wiki/t/Frame)).
- **Animation craft:** use strong key poses, a short anticipation, smears and overshoot ([Cartwright, GDC 2014](https://gdcvault.com/play/1020971/)), and a hit-stop freeze on impact ([Sakurai on hitstop](https://sourcegaming.info/2015/11/11/thoughts-on-hitstop-sakurais-famitsu-column-vol-490-1/)).
- **Fight Night and Undisputed:** their timing data was NOT FOUND.

**Suggested jab at 30 fps (estimate), 13–18 frames, about 0.43–0.6 s:**
- 1–2 frames loading the hip and shoulder
- 3–4 frames of extension, with a smear or motion blur
- 2–3 frames of hit-stop
- 7–9 frames easing back to guard

That matches the 0.52 s measured for a whole jab.

## 4. Spacing
- **Measured:** 1.23 ± 0.16 m between the boxers ([ECSS 2023](https://www.ecss.mobi/DATA/EDSS/C28/28-2883.pdf), 33 French elite boxers). The game's 0.557 m is 45% of that, more than 4 standard deviations below the mean.
- **Jab range (estimate):** about 0.9–1.1 m chest to chest, from a reach of about 1.78 m.
- **Hook range (estimate):** about 0.6–0.75 m.
- **Clinch (estimate):** about 0.25–0.35 m, chests touching. This is the only state where under 0.5 m is legitimate.
- **How games stop torsos merging:** each fighter has a separate pushbox that only collides with the other fighter's pushbox. Overlap is split 50/50 along the line between the fighters, and any leftover goes to the fighter who isn't cornered ([Press Button Win](https://www.pressbuttonwin.com/p/why-did-that-miss), [Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/hitboxes-and-hurtboxes-in-unity)). In 3D, give each boxer a vertical capsule and resolve it every tick, after animation and before foot IK.

## 5. Fix first, in order
1. **Minimum spacing (pushbox).** This fixes the merging, red's lean, and part of the twist.
   - Give each boxer a capsule of radius about 0.22–0.28 m.
   - Preferred AI range: about 1.0–1.25 m between exchanges, 0.65–0.75 m for hooks, and under 0.5 m only in a clinch state.
   - An animator would author spacing into each move: step in on the jab and hook, then step out.
2. **Lock planted feet with step triggers.** This fixes the 13–15% slide and the gliding.
   - Lock the ball of each planted foot in world space, allowing only a heel lift or a pivot on the ball (rear foot on the cross, lead foot on the hook).
   - When the root drifts more than about 0.15 m from a foot, trigger a 4–6-frame step instead of a slide.
   - Cap the root at 1.5 m/s outside authored lunges.
   - An animator would author step clips with foot-contact curves and use their root motion.
3. **Punch timing curve and posture targets.** This fixes the "bullet" jab and the twist.
   - Use the 13–18-frame jab from section 3.
   - Drive rotation from the pelvis and cap the twist between shoulders and pelvis at about 30° (estimate).
   - Hold hip height at about 0.80–0.88 m for a 1.78 m boxer (scaled by height) and feet 0.45–0.75 m apart, crouching below 0.70 m only on ducks and slips.
   - Put shoes on both boxers and match blue's posture to red's.

**Not found and marked as estimates:** measured stance width, stance hip height, step-jab length, foot pivot angles, and Fight Night or Undisputed timing.

The S262 research on MetaHuman body correctives is running now. I'll paste the full answer here when it's done, including the UE Python steps, asset names, RBF parameters and risks.

**S262: MetaHuman body correctives in UE 5.8 (part 1 of 3)**

Short answer: for UE 5.6+ MetaHumans, the body helper joints are driven by RBF solvers stored in the **body DNA** and evaluated by **RigLogic**. They are not driven by AnimGraph Pose Driver nodes. Epic's open-source **OpenRigLogic** (MIT, with a `5.8` branch and Python bindings) runs the same evaluation outside UE. That means you can read every solver straight from the DNA and port it to Godot exactly, so you may not need grid sampling at all. I ran no UE or Godot code, so every code sketch is untested. Sources are tagged S1 to S11, with the list in part 3. Anything I couldn't verify is marked GUESS.

**Q1. Where body correctives are evaluated (5.6 to 5.8)**
- **They're RBF solvers in the body DNA, run by RigLogic.** The Body Conform doc says "Auto Rig Helper Joints … helper joints will be repositioned … and RBF weights will be recalculated" and "Helper joints and RBFs will remain unchanged from the current MetaHuman state", so the RBFs are part of the character's data (S2). OpenRigLogic says DCC Export produces "a DNA file for the head and a DNA file for the body, the inputs needed to drive the character … same runtime rig evaluation as Unreal Engine" (S4).
- **The DNA has an RBF layer, `RBFBehaviorReader`** (S4a). Per solver it exposes getRBFSolverCount, Name, Type, Radius, AutomaticRadius, WeightThreshold, DistanceMethod, NormalizeMethod, FunctionType, TwistAxis, RawControlIndices, RawControlValues and PoseIndices. Per pose it exposes getRBFPoseName, JointOutputIndices, JointOutputValues, Scale, InputControlIndices, OutputControlIndices and OutputControlWeights. There's also a separate joint-behaviour layer.
- **Epic staff confirm the switch.** For "MetaHuman Creator in Unreal Engine 5.6, or … UERBFSolvers", Epic recommends "Pose Editor from the MetaHuman for Maya plugin instead of Pose Driver Connect … for the performance gains" (Chris Theodosius, Epic, forum post of 2025-08-21, S3).
- **The runtime switch is on the MetaHuman component.** It has "Enable Body Correctives" ("Preserves the volume and realistic skin deformations …"), with an LOD threshold that defaults to **LOD0 only**. Each body part also has an optional "Control Rig Class … Evaluation happens after the base skeleton gets evaluated as a post-process". The neck has its own "Neck Correctives (pose drivers)" and "Neck Procedural Control Rig" (S1).
- **Older MetaHumans (Bridge, before 5.6) worked differently.** Their helper joints were driven by Pose Driver nodes in a post-process AnimBP that is set on the skeletal mesh and runs after the main AnimBP (S11). The asset names I remember, `ABP_Body_PostProcess` and `ABP_Face_PostProcess` under /Game/MetaHumans/Common/, are a GUESS that I didn't verify this session.
- **The exact 5.6+ asset and class names are GUESS.** That covers the `MetaHumanCharacter` plugin and asset, the assembled `BP_<Name>`, a `UMetaHumanComponentBody`-style component, and a RigLogic AnimNode such as `FAnimNode_RigLogic`. Step 1 of the run list checks them in MHPilot.

**Q2. Running it headless and reading helper transforms (most reliable first)**
- **A. OpenRigLogic Python on the body DNA (recommended).** It's pure CPU, so it's headless by construction and needs no UE at runtime. Build it from `git clone -b 5.8` with CMake, SWIG and Python dev headers (S4 README). Get `body.dna` from MetaHuman Creator **Export > DCC Export** (S4). Untested sketch, with API names from S4c and S4a:
```python
import dna, riglogic, json
s = dna.FileStream("body.dna", dna.FileStream.AccessMode_Read, dna.FileStream.OpenMode_Binary)
r = dna.BinaryStreamReader(s, dna.DataLayer_All); r.read(); assert dna.Status.isOk()
rl = riglogic.RigLogic(r); ri = riglogic.RigInstance(rl)
names = [r.getRawControlName(i) for i in range(r.getRawControlCount())]  # GUESS method name
# set driver-joint local rotation quats (relative to neutral: GUESS convention)
for i, v in my_pose_controls.items(): ri.setRawControl(i, v)
rl.calculate(ri)
out = ri.getJointOutputs()  # per joint 9 or 10 attrs (t, r[q], s): GUESS layout
```
The basic calls come from Epic's `demo.py`. The control-name lookup, the output layout and the input convention are GUESS.
- **B. Tick a mesh in an editor world.** Spawn the assembled BP or a SkeletalMeshActor, pose it with a one-frame AnimSequence or a PoseableMesh, tick it, then read `get_socket_transform(bone, unreal.RelativeTransformSpace.RTS_PARENT_BONE_SPACE)`. Under `-run=pythonscript` no level ticks, so you'd have to force the animation update, which makes this route unreliable. The mesh also needs `AlwaysTickPoseAndRefreshBones` and correctives at LOD0. Whether this works with `-nullrhi` is a GUESS: RigLogic itself is CPU-only, so the risk is the component ticking in a commandlet.

Bake through Sequencer with the post-process left on.** A tutorial warns that baking with the post-process on bakes the correctives in, causing the "double offset" problem (S11), and that's exactly what you want here. The 5.8 API is GUESS, and it probably needs an editor that can render (GUESS).
- **D. Control Rig Python** (`ControlRigBlueprint`, `RigHierarchy`). This only applies if the correctives lived in a Control Rig, and the body Control Rig slot is optional (S1) and probably empty by default (GUESS). Not recommended.

**S262 (part 2 of 3): reading the RBF data, and the RBF math**

**Q3. Reading the solver data directly**
- **From the DNA, everything is readable** through `RBFBehaviorReader` (S4a, method list in Q1) via the SWIG `dna` Python module (S4).
  - Per solver you get the type, the radius, automatic radius, the threshold, the distance method, the normalize method, the function and the twist axis. You also get the raw control values, which are the target poses flattened, and the pose indices.
  - Radius is converted between degrees and radians on load, via angConv in `CPURBFBehaviorFactory.h` (S4b).
  - Per pose you get the joint output indices and values (the helper-joint deltas), the scale, and the output control weights.
- **From the older Pose Driver nodes:** `unreal.RBFParams` exposes `solver_type`, `radius`, `automatic_radius`, `function`, `distance_method`, `twist_axis`, `weight_threshold`, `normalize_method`, `median_reference`, `median_min` and `median_max` (S5).
  - Reaching the node inside an AnimBP graph from Python isn't documented. `AnimGraphNode_PoseDriver` and the runtime `FAnimNode_PoseDriver`, with members like `RBFParams`, `PoseTargets` and `SourceBones`, aren't exposed through the standard Python graph APIs.
  - GUESS: you'd need a small C++ helper, or to copy the node out as text (a T3D paste).

**Q4. The RBF math to port**
- **UE AnimGraph enums** (`/Engine/Source/Runtime/AnimGraphRuntime/Public/RBF/RBFSolver.h`, S5 and S6):
  - RBFFunctionType: Gaussian 0, Exponential 1, Linear 2, Cubic 3, Quintic 4, DefaultFunction 5.
  - RBFNormalizeMethod has four values:
    - OnlyNormalizeAboveOne 0.
    - AlwaysNormalize 1.
    - NormalizeWithinMedian 2: a "cone with min and max angle within which the value will be interpolated between non-normalized and normalized".
    - NoNormalization 3: "only with interpolative … inputs within area bounded by targets".
  - RBFDistanceMethod: Euclidean, Quaternion, SwingAngle, TwistAngle, DefaultMethod.
- **The DNA/RigLogic version** has only OnlyNormalizeAboveOne and AlwaysNormalize, and no Default* values (S4 RBFBehavior docs page).
- **Exact formulas from OpenRigLogic's `RBFSolver.cpp`** (S4b). Here d is the distance and r is the radius, which the source calls kernelWidth.
  - **Distance:**
    - Euclidean: \( d = \sqrt{\sum (t_i - x_i)^2} \).
    - Quaternion: per quaternion, \( \text{arc} = \arccos(2\,(q_a \cdot q_b)^2 - 1) \), or 0 if dot² > 1; then \( d = \sqrt{\sum \text{arc}^2} \). Inputs must be normalized.
    - SwingAngle: reduce the input and the targets to their swing part about the twist axis, then use the Quaternion arc.
    - TwistAngle: zero the non-twist components, renormalize (twist, w), unwind the angle into [−π, π], and use \( d = \sqrt{\sum \Delta\text{angle}^2} \). The jump at ±180° is deliberate, and a source comment says it matches UE's `FQuat::GetTwistAngle`.
  - **Kernels:**
    - Gaussian \( w = e^{-d/r^2} \). Note that d is **not** squared, exactly as in the source.
    - Exponential \( w = e^{-2d/r} \).
    - Linear \( w = \max(0, 1 - d/r) \).
    - Cubic \( w = \max(0, 1 - (d/r)^3) \).
    - Quintic \( w = \max(0, 1 - (d/r)^5) \).
  - **Automatic radius** is the mean distance over all N(N−1)/2 pairs of targets.
  - **Additive solver:** \( w_i = \text{kernel}(d_i) \), then normalize and cut off.
  - **Interpolative solver:** build the N×N matrix \( A_{ij} = \text{kernel}(\text{dist}(t_i, t_j)) \), diagonal included, and invert it with LU. At runtime \( w = \text{clamp}(A^{-1}\varphi(x), 0, 1) \) per element, then normalize and cut off.
  - **Normalize and cut off:** let s = Σw. The ratio is 1/s if s > 1 or the method is AlwaysNormalize; otherwise it's 1. Then \( w_i \leftarrow w_i \cdot \text{ratio} \cdot \text{poseScale}_i \), and \( w_i = 0 \) if it's at or below weightThreshold.
  - **Output:** helper joint = neutral + Σ (pose weight × that pose's jointOutputValues). This is a GUESS: the exact composition, meaning per-attribute additive deltas and how rotations combine, lives in `src/riglogic/rbf/RBFBehaviorOutputInstance.cpp`. Read it before porting.
- **Not verified:** that UE's own AnimGraph `FRBFSolver` uses the same kernels, and the NormalizeWithinMedian maths. My GUESS is that they match, since the TwistAngle comment claims parity with UE.

**S262 (part 3 of 3): licence, run list, parameters, risks, sources**

**Q5. Licence**
- **Other engines are allowed.** "We've updated the Unreal Engine EULA so MetaHuman characters and animation can be used in any engine, such as Unity or Godot" (S8). The licence page says "MetaHuman is included as part of your standard Unreal Engine license … free to use for anyone making under $1 million USD … MetaHumans can be used with any engine or creative software" (S7).
- **FAQ, quoted second-hand via S9.** The FAQ answers on metahuman.com are collapsed and wouldn't load.
  - "MetaHuman characters and animation are classed as Non-Engine Products under the Unreal Engine EULA, so neither their use as linear media output or at runtime in games … using engines other than Unreal Engine triggers royalty obligations."
  - "If you make over $1 million USD in annual gross revenue and render MetaHuman characters and animation outside of Unreal Engine, you'll need an Unreal Engine seat license."
  - On AI, you may use MetaHumans in "workflows that incorporate artificial intelligence technology", but not to train or enhance AI models.
- **Your helper-joint table** is rig data derived from a 5.6+ MetaHuman body. It is very likely covered as part of the character you ship in Godot. That's a GUESS and not legal advice: the FAQ talks about "characters and animation", and I found no wording about rig-data tables. Check the EULA's Non-Engine Products text, and never feed this data into AI training.
- **OpenRigLogic is MIT** (GitHub spdx MIT, S4). Using it to evaluate or port the solvers is fine. Keep the MIT notice if you ship ported code.
- **Don't use MetaHuman-DNA-Calibration** (S10).
  - Its licence is proprietary: "license to reproduce and prepare derivative works … for the sole purpose of developing and using tools that enable third-party software programs to export and edit digital characters … You may not distribute the Software".
  - Characters made with it "may only be used in conjunction with Unreal Engine".
  - Its README says it "has not been updated to support MetaHuman characters created in … 5.6".

**Run list (all untested)**
1. **Probe in UE.** This is asset reads only, so headless is fine. Add it to `mh_probe.py`:
```python
import unreal
sk = unreal.load_asset("/Game/MetaHumans/<Name>/Body/<BodyMesh>")  # GUESS path
print(sk.get_editor_property("post_process_anim_blueprint"))
for a in unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.list_assets("/Game/MetaHumans", recursive=True):
    if any(k in a for k in ("DNA", "RigLogic", "ABP", "PostProcess")): print(a)
```
2. **Get `body.dna`** from MetaHuman Creator **Export > DCC Export** (S4). The alternative is the DNA asset in the body mesh's asset user data (`UDNAAsset`, GUESS).
3. **Build OpenRigLogic** from the `5.8` branch with its Python wrappers (CMake + SWIG), and run `demo.py` on `body.dna` (S4c).
4. **Dump the solvers to JSON** with `RBFBehaviorReader`. Keep the ones whose pose joint outputs touch lowerarm_*, upperarm_*, clavicle_* and the twist joints.
5. **Pick one route:**
   - (a) Port the exact solver to Godot (GDScript or C#, using the Q4 formulas). Its inputs are the driver joints' local quats relative to neutral (GUESS convention; step 6 checks it).
   - (b) Sample your grid through `riglogic` (elbow 0/30/60/90/120/145 × roll −60/0/+60, plus the shoulder grid) and write the helper transforms to JSON.
6. **Validate a few poses** against UE using route B (with a viewport if needed). Compare parent-space helper transforms to a tolerance of 1e-3 cm and 0.05°.

**RBF parameters:** read them from the DNA rather than assuming them. The only fields defined (S4a) are type, radius, automaticRadius, weightThreshold, distanceMethod, normalizeMethod, function and twistAxis. Typical MetaHuman values (Quaternion or Swing distance, Gaussian, Interpolative) are a GUESS.

**Risks**
- The 5.6+ asset and class names are unverified, and the older Pose Driver names don't apply to 5.6+ characters.
- Headless UE ticking (routes B and C) may never run the correctives, so prefer OpenRigLogic.
- The input convention still needs checking: local versus neutral-relative quaternions, axis order, units, and the per-LOD solver lists (`getRBFSolverIndicesForLOD`).
- The UE-to-Godot change (Z-up cm to Y-up m) has to be applied to both inputs and outputs.
- TwistAngle jumps at ±180°, by design.
- In UE, body correctives default to LOD0 only (S1).
- The licence wording for rig tables is unconfirmed, and AI training is prohibited.

**Sources**

- S2 [Body Conform Controls doc](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/metahuman/body-conform-controls)
- S3 [Pose Driver Connect forum thread, page 4](https://forums.unrealengine.com/t/tutorial-authoring-secondary-animation-in-maya-and-unreal-with-pose-driver-connect/1496699?page=4)
- S4 [OpenRigLogic on GitHub](https://github.com/EpicGames/OpenRigLogic) and its [docs](https://epicgames.github.io/OpenRigLogic/), plus the source files `RBFBehaviorReader.h`, `RBFSolver.cpp`, `InterpolativeRBFSolver.cpp`, `AdditiveRBFSolver.cpp`, `CPURBFBehaviorFactory.h` and `demo.py`
- S5 [UE 5.8 Python RBFParams](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/python-api/class/RBFParams)
- S6 [FRBFSolver C++ API](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/API/Runtime/AnimGraphRuntime/FRBFSolver)
- S7 [MetaHuman licence page](https://www.metahuman.com/license)
- S8 [State of Unreal 2025 news](https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/news/all-the-big-news-and-announcements-from-the-state-of-unreal-2025)

- S10 MetaHuman-DNA-Calibration README and LICENSE on GitHub
